You use the simple future (andrò, sarò, avrò, farò) for plans and predictions, "quando" and "se" with the future, and the future of probability (Saranno le otto).
In August we'll go to Sibiu.
When you arrive, I'll call you.
If the weather's nice, we'll go to the mountains.
In twenty years I'll be an astronaut.
Where's Giulia? — She must still be in bed.
To form the future of regular verbs: parlerò, prenderò, partirò.
To use the irregular future: sarò, avrò, andrò, farò, verrò, vorrò, potrò.
To use "quando" and "appena" + future: Quando arriverai, ti chiamerò.
To make real hypotheses with "se" + present or future.
To express a guess with the future of probability: Saranno le otto.
To talk about holiday plans and the distant future.
A May evening on the terrace of Giulia's new flat. She and Matei are looking at the calendar.
So, what shall we do this summer?
In August the workshop will close for three weeks. Shall we go to Sibiu?
Yes! At last I'll meet your parents. But… I'll be so nervous.
Don't worry. My mother will adore you and my father will make you taste his pălincă.
And the tickets? Shall we fly from Pisa or from Bologna?
From Bologna, it's cheaper. I'll book them tomorrow, when I get my salary.
And what will we do in Romania?
We'll stay a week in Sibiu. Then, if the weather's nice, we'll go to the mountains, the Făgăraș. You'll love it, you'll see.
The mountains? I'm Neapolitan: for me the mountains means Vesuvius!
Then afterwards we'll go to the seaside, to Costinești. The Black Sea isn't the Bay of Naples, but…
But you'll be there. All right. And in September?
In September, who knows… Bellini said he'll have important news for me. I don't know what it will be.
It must be something good. Bellini never gives bad news… only work!
"ti farà assaggiare" = will make you taste
The future is stressed on the LAST syllable for io and lui: par-le-RÒ, sa-RÀ. The written accent shows you this.
For noi and voi the stress is on "RE": an-DRE-mo, sa-RE-te. Not an-dre-MO!
For loro: sa-RAN-no, an-DRAN-no, with a double N.
CH + i = "kee": kis-SÀ, stressed at the end, with a double S.
Take the infinitive without the final -e and add: -ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno. -ARE verbs change A to E: parlare → parlerò.
Spelling: -care / -gare add an H (cercherò, pagherò), -ciare / -giare drop the I (comincerò, mangerò).
Many common verbs shorten their stem. The endings stay the same:
Venire, volere, bere, rimanere have a double RR: verrò, vorrò, berrò, rimarrò.
In Italian, after "quando" (when) and "appena" (as soon as), if the meaning is future, you use the future too — just like Romanian ("când vei ajunge"):
As soon as I get my salary, I'll book the tickets.
With "se" (if) you can use the present or the future; both are correct:
If the weather's nice, we go to the mountains.
Unlike English, you DON'T use the present after "quando" with a future meaning: "Quando arrivi" is accepted in speech, but "Quando arriverai" is the correct, elegant form.
Italians also use the future to make a GUESS about the present, like Romanian "o fi", "o avea":
Che ore sono? — Saranno le otto.
What time is it? — It must be about eight.
Dov'è Giulia? — Sarà ancora a letto.
Quanti anni ha il signor Franco? — Avrà ottant'anni.
How old is Signor Franco? — He must be about eighty.
Pietro isn't eating. He must be tired.
It's very common in conversation. When you hear a future about NOW, it means "probably".
For definite, near plans Italians often use the present: "Domani parto per Roma." The future is preferred for:
Ti piacerà. Te lo prometto: arriverò in orario.
In ten years Pietro will be eighteen.
Will you come to the party?
When you get to Florence, I'll call you.
What time is it? — It must be about nine.
Will you know what to do?
"If it rains, we'll stay at home."
Per quanto tempo chiuderà il laboratorio ad agosto?
Dove andranno se farà bel tempo?
Che cosa avrà Bellini a settembre?

In May Pietro's teacher set a special task: "Write a letter to yourselves in twenty years' time. We'll put it in a box and open it in 2045." Pietro worked all afternoon in the trattoria. Here is his letter.

"Dear Pietro of the future, when you read this letter you'll be twenty-eight. How strange! You'll be tall, maybe you'll have a beard like Grandpa Aldo in the photos. I hope you won't have big ears like Dad.

You'll definitely be an astronaut. You'll go to Mars and take a photo of Florence with you, so the Martians will see the most beautiful city in the world. If there's no pistachio ice cream on Mars, you'll come straight back.

Grandma will be ninety-two. She'll still be in the kitchen, I'm sure, and she'll still make ribollita on Fridays. She'll never retire. When I tell her to rest, she'll answer: 'I'll rest when I'm dead.' She always says that.
Michelangelo the cat, sadly, won't be around any more. But maybe I'll have another cat and call him Michelangelo the Second.

Matei and Giulia will be married. I know because I saw them kissing behind the fountain in Santo Spirito, and when two people kiss behind a fountain, they get married. They'll have three children. One will speak Romanian, one Neapolitan and one Florentine, and they'll never understand each other.

Professor Bellini will be very old and will still say "bene" only once a year. Signor Franco… will be a hundred and ten, but I think he'll still be in his shop, because he doesn't get older: he's always been old.

Ilinca, Matei's sister, will come to Florence every summer and will finally know how to make ribollita without too much salt. Gennaro will still have the little red car, because that car will never die, like tortoises. And he'll still drive with one hand.

Dear Pietro, I'm asking you for three promises. One: you'll never forget the trattoria. Two: you'll always do your homework (that one's for Grandma, who's reading over my shoulder). Three: when you're grown up, you'll give a watch to a child who's always late, like Matei did for me.
See you in 2045. Greetings from the past, Pietro (8 and three quarters)."

Graziella read the letter twice. Then she went into the kitchen and for a while nobody heard her. When she came back, her eyes were red. "It must be the onions," she said. But that day there was nothing with onions on the menu.

Write (10–12 sentences) a letter to yourself in ten years' time: where you'll live, what you'll do, who you'll be with, what languages you'll speak. Use "quando" and "se" with the future and at least one guess.
I used at least eight verbs in the future.
I used at least three irregular verbs (sarò, avrò, andrò, farò…).
I used the future of probability (sarà…, avrà…).
Dear future me, in ten years I'll be forty-five.
I'll speak Italian very well and maybe I'll live in Tuscany.
When I have more time, I'll learn Japanese too.
If all goes well, I'll have a little house with a garden. My children will already be grown up.
